endorsements.title: Guardrails for GenAI drafted replies in patient portal messaging
endorsements.issuer: Sakr J. npj Digital Medicine 2026;9 (PMID 41942581, doi:10.1038/s41746-026-02621-6)
endorsements.quote: Where systems are designed in ways that predictably encourage automation complacency, governance, not individual vigilance, must carry the corrective burden5.

evidence.title: Evaluating the Large Language Model-Based Quality Assurance Tool for Auto-Contouring
evidence.outcome: Error-detection (sensitivity/specificity) of LLM-based QA screening of auto-contours against radiation oncologist ground truth
evidence.effect: Weighted kappa 0.730–0.798 across software; cutoff ≥4 gave highest sensitivity in rectum (0.976) and highest specificity in left femoral head (0.933); potential overestimation bias risks missing inadequate cases.
evidence.quote: A cutoff of ≥4 as “adequate “ narrowed the CIs, yielding the highest sensitivity in the rectum (0.976) and the highest specificity in the left femoral head (0.933).
evidence.sample_unit: male pelvic CT scans (auto-contours from three software packages; 291 rationale outputs rated)

evidence.title: Extracting Clinical Guideline Information Using Two Large Language Models: Evaluation Study
evidence.outcome: Error rate among LLM-agreed cases versus expert labels, and manual review reduction
evidence.effect: Consistent predictions for 341 of 385 items, reducing manual review by 88.6%; only one (0.3%) agreed-upon case diverged from expert labels. Threshold strategy cut priority review to 2.9% (11/385), error rate 0.5% (2/374).
evidence.quote: Among these agreed-upon cases, only one (0.3%) diverged from expert labels.

evidence.title: Digital Pathology with AI for Cervical Biopsies: Diagnostic Accuracy at the CIN2+ Threshold
evidence.outcome: Whether pathologist review corrects AI errors in ACIS and suspected SCC calls
evidence.effect: After adjudication (EE + P2), ACIS restored from 13/20 to 18/20 and SCC calls reduced from 4 to 1 of 20; 6 of 7 AI-flagged SCC in P1-CIN3 retained.
evidence.quote: After expert adjudication in the EE + P2 condition, ACIS was restored to 18/20 and SCC was reduced to 1/20, demonstrating that the human reviewer corrected virtually all high-consequence AI errors.

evidence.title: Next-generation multicenter studies: using artificial intelligence to automatically process unstructured health records of patients with lung cancer across multiple institutions
evidence.venue: Annals of oncology : official journal of the European Society for Medical Oncology
evidence.outcome: Error rate reduction with targeted human review of low-confidence AI outputs
evidence.effect: Targeted human review of 30% of low-confidence AI outputs decreased error rates to 4.4%
evidence.quote: A hybrid approach with targeted human review of 30% of low-confidence AI outputs further decreased error rates to 4.4%.

evidence.title: End-to-End Pipeline Integrating Local Small Language Models and Machine Learning for Data Extraction and Stroke Outcome Prediction in Emergency Department
evidence.outcome: Error-detection yield of human review by flag tier and random sample of unflagged records
evidence.effect: HITL reviewed 289 records: cosine-flagged 62.4% had errors, RAG-fallback 78.6%, random nonflagged 3.8%; accuracy rose 86.0% to 97.0% after HITL.
evidence.quote: Among these, 93 records were flagged by cosine similarity (58 contained at least one extraction error, 62.4%), 14 by the RAG fallback mechanism (11 contained errors, 78.6%), and 182 were randomly sampled nonflagged records (7 contained errors, 3.8%).

commentary.bottom_line: Five offline studies measured how well AI screening or human review caught AI errors, and three of them routed review by model agreement, confidence, or flag tier and reported lower residual error rates after targeted review. All five used retrospective or simulated designs outside live care, so the evidence suggests that tier-level measurement is feasible but offers little certainty about how review tiers perform in deployment.

perspectives.view: All five studies are level 4, retrospective or descriptive, and run offline. Samples range from 20 CT scans to 1,166 records. Tasks span contouring, pharmacogenomics, pathology, and clinical records, and only three assigned review by risk tier. None tested tiered review prospectively or in live care. Indirectness and risk of bias lower certainty to very low.

In the Korean records study, 62.4% of cosine-flagged and 78.6% of RAG-fallback records had errors, compared with 3.8% of randomly sampled unflagged records. That residual rate suggests the low-risk tier may need its own random audit. The contouring study reported that overestimation bias could let inadequate cases pass LLM screening.

Error measurement in these studies depended on expert ground-truth labels assembled for research. In the pathology study, adjudicated review restored ACIS calls from 13 of 20 to 18 of 20 and reduced SCC calls from 4 to 1. No study tested whether teams can sustain this kind of labeling within routine clinical workflows.

In the pharmacogenomics study, model agreement cut manual review by 88.6%, and a threshold strategy sent 11 of 385 items (2.9%) to priority review with a 0.5% error rate in the remainder. In the French study, reviewing the 30% of outputs with lowest confidence lowered error rates to 4.4%. No study reported staffing time or cost.

One study used clinical records from South Korea, which the map tags as non-English. No study drew on Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, and none reported error-detection rates by patient subgroup. Tier thresholds validated on these datasets may not hold for records from under-resourced settings.

commentary.research_gap: No study measured error-detection rates by review tier in a live clinical deployment, tracked how those rates change over time, or tested whether adjusting tiers based on measured rates reduced the number of errors reaching patients. Prospective studies that include random audits of low-risk tiers, report results by patient subgroup, and record reviewer time and cost would address these gaps.
commentary.underserved_note: The South Korean clinical records study used non-English records, and it is the only test tagged for a language population. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, or patients with limited English proficiency in US care settings. Health systems serving these groups will need to measure tier-level detection rates in their own patient populations rather than rely on published thresholds.
